title: Family land and a lawyer's theft in New Orleans
summary: Levy describes his Choctaw grandmother's land and his father's property sold to a railroad. After his father's death a lawyer pocketed the money, and his mother went home to sort it out.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Grandmother's family, some of them married, one of them married an Italian, another married a Frenchman, and somebody married a Jewish fellow. Well, you see, those days you're on, women were kind of scarce, I guess, and there was a whole lot more men, yes, a whole lot more men than there were women. My mother was a full, my grandmother was a full-blooded Indian, and they have a little piece of land that the government gave the Indians way back in history when they moved them. She was from Georgia. I think she was a Choctaw. Well, anyhow, the government gave them this land along the Mississippi, and she has 45 living descendants now. I'm one of the living descendants, and we get, I think, we get about $16 a year from this land. You see, it's all land, and there's only one place rented, and so we get $16 a year, and 45 living descendants.
You mentioned having a lot of land at one time in New Orleans. Had your father been?

Yes, yes, he had bought a lot, and for little or nothing, and they built that railroad terminal on it, so the people, so he sold it and made quite a bit of money. And then he bought other pieces of property, and after my father died, my mother put it in the hands of a lawyer, and the lawyer started putting the money in the pocket, and the bed went from voice, and we lost it finally.
Was your mother in New Orleans at the time you were up here at school?

Well, we were up here, and then when she found out about this lawyer appropriating the money and putting it in his pocket, she jumped on the train and went down there to straighten it out. She had to mortgage one piece of property and sell another piece of property because she had to take care of herself and send me some money, too, and then she had to straighten all the tax mess out, and there was, I guess, a lien on the property for the improvement. They were doing away with the gutters. You know, the gutters were kind of bad in those days. They were doing it. So there was quite a bit of money involved, and so it cost us quite a bit to straighten this stuff out.
That was the source of your income when you started school?
Was your father alive at that time?
